Spare
spair
v. (to withhold a deserved stroke; to refrain from destroying; rendering Hebrew chamal and chus, Greek pheidomai)
From the Saxon sparian, to spare or save. Hebrew chamal means to pity or spare; chus, to have compassion, literally to let the eye flow. To spare in Hebrew is an act of the eye before it is an act of the hand.

Biblical Definition

To spare is to withhold a stroke that was deserved or intended, and Scripture's use of the word reaches its centre in one verse: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The whole argument for Christian assurance is compressed into an inference from the greater to the lesser. God did not spare where sparing would have cost him most; therefore no lesser gift will be withheld. The Greek echoes Genesis 22, where Abraham is told thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son — and the difference is that at the last moment a ram was provided for Isaac, and for Christ there was no substitute, because he was the substitute. God is also said to spare, and the image is domestic: “I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him” (Malachi 3:17), spoken of those who feared the LORD and spake often one to another. Jonah ends on a question about sparing a pagan city of six score thousand who could not discern their right hand from their left (Jonah 4:11). And Proverbs applies the word to a father's rod: “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes” (Proverbs 13:24) — sparing is not always kindness.

Webster 1828 Definition

To withhold a deserved stroke. God spared not his own Son, and every lesser gift follows from it; he spares his people as a father his son; and Proverbs warns that a spared rod is not love.

expand to see more

SPARE, v.t. [Sax. sparian.] To use frugally; not to be profuse; to use with moderation.

2. To save or withhold from any particular use or occupation; as, to spare time from business.

3. To omit; to forbear; as, to spare a rebuke.

4. To use tenderly; to treat with pity and forbearance; to forbear to afflict, punish or destroy.

5. To part with without inconvenience; as, he can spare a shilling.

Key Scripture

Romans 8:32 — "He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?"

Malachi 3:17 — "And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him."

Proverbs 13:24 — "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes."

Jonah 4:11 — "And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?"

Modern Corruption

Sparing is treated as the whole of love, so that discipline of children and church alike is thought unkind — and God's not sparing his own Son is softened into a tragedy rather than a purpose.

expand to see more

Proverbs 13:24 states an unfashionable principle in the plainest terms: withholding correction is hatred, and correcting early is love. Scripture's doctrine of discipline is not harshness — fathers are expressly commanded not to provoke their children to wrath, and correction is betimes, that is, early and proportionate, not violent or late. But the modern assumption that any correction wounds a child inverts the verse and produces exactly the child the proverb warns of. The same instinct empties church discipline, which Scripture commands for the good of the offender, and turns pastoral care into unconditional affirmation. Hebrews 12 makes the argument decisive: the Lord chastens whom he loves, and a son not chastened is not a son. The other softening runs the other way. Romans 8:32 is sometimes preached as though the cross were something that happened to God rather than something he purposed, but the verb is active: he… delivered him up. The Father gave, the Son gave himself, and the atonement was not an accident of history but a definite and effectual purpose to save a definite people.

The principle to recover is the argument in Romans 8:32, which is the strongest logic in the Bible for a doubting Christian. The reasoning is not that God is generally kind but that a specific and infinitely costly thing has already been done. If the Son was not spared, no argument remains for supposing that anything smaller will be denied to those for whom he was given. Assurance built here does not depend on a believer's feelings, and Paul goes on to say that nothing in the whole creation shall separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chamal is to spare or pity; chus, to have compassion, literally of the eye. Greek pheidomai is to spare or forbear, the verb of Romans 8:32.

expand to see more

Hebrew chamal (H2550) — to spare, to have compassion; used of Pharaoh's daughter and of God.

Hebrew chus (H2347) — to pity, to spare; literally to let the eye flow with compassion.

Greek pheidomai (G5339) — to spare, to refrain; he that spared not his own Son.

Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver up, to hand over; the Father's act in Romans 8:32.

Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to withhold; thou hast not withheld thy son, Genesis 22:12.

Usage

"Of the Son not spared: he that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32)."

"Of God sparing his own: I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him (Malachi 3:17)."

"Of a rod not to be spared: he that spareth his rod hateth his son (Proverbs 13:24)."
